title: Metallogeny of the Mesoproterozoic Belt-Purcell Basin, Northern Rocky Mountains, USA-Canada
abstract: Abstract Metasedimentary rocks of the Mesoproterozoic Belt Supergroup in the United States and correlative Purcell Supergroup in Canada contain diverse types of mineral deposits with a variety of commodities including base metals, precious metals, and critical metals. The economically most important deposits (≥ 10 Mt past production + reserves + resources) are stratabound Pb–Zn–Ag ores at the Sullivan mine in southeastern British Columbia, Ag–Pb–Zn–(Cu) veins of the Coeur d’Alene district in northern Idaho, stratabound sediment-hosted Cu–Ag deposits of the Spar Lake, Montanore, and Rock Creek deposits in western Montana, stratabound Co–Cu–Au–(Bi–Y–REE) ores of the Idaho cobalt belt, and stratiform Cu–Co–Ag at the Black Butte deposit in western Montana. Minor deposits in the region, also hosted in strata of the Belt and Purcell supergroups, are stratabound Pb–Zn–Ag deposits in southeastern British Columbia, and Th–REE–(Cu) veins of the Lemhi Pass district in northern Idaho and western Montana. Small prospects and occurrences include gold-quartz veins, Ag–Pb–Zn veins, Fe–(Cu–Au) deposits, and a variety of rare metals (Th, REE, Nb, Be, Sn) in pegmatites and carbonatites. High-precision geochronology of ore and gangue minerals, like in the Sullivan deposit, has yielded only Mesoproterozoic ages, but other deposits (Blackbird, Rock Creek, Coeur d’Alene, Lemhi Pass) have U–Pb and/or Re–Os ages that suggest Neoproterozoic, Paleozoic, and/or Mesozoic to Tertiary overprinting of older Mesoproterozoic mineralization, possibly linked in some cases to fluid flow during reactivation of deep basement structures. Some of the Paleozoic and younger ages are also attributed here to dissolution-reprecipitation of dated minerals and not to new metal introduction. An integrated assessment of the geochronological data reveals growing evidence for previously underappreciated roles of major mineralizing events occurring during the East Kootenay orogeny (1379 − 1325 Ma) and the Grenvillian orogeny (1150 to 980 Ma), with important implications for mineral exploration in many parts of the Belt-Purcell Basin.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The Mesoproterozoic Belt-Purcell Basin in the northern Rocky Mountains contains diverse types of mineral deposits (e.g., Lydon  91 ; Box et al.  21 ). This overview is focused on the metallogeny of metallic deposits, prospects, and occurrences in strata of the Belt and Purcell supergroups of known or possible Mesoproterozoic age, emphasizing those with major past production, reserves, and/or resources. For the purposes of this report, major and minor deposits, districts, and other occurrences are those having a minimum of 10 Mt of ore or mineralized rock; minor deposits, prospects, and occurrences have less, or none. Excluded from discussion are younger (Cretaceous to early Tertiary) deposits such as the polymetallic vein and porphyry ores of the Butte district and the breccia and vein gold ores of the Golden Sunlight mine (Whitehall district), both in Montana, and most Ag–Pb–Zn veins in the region. Non-metallic deposits and placers (Au, REE) also are not discussed.

This paper summarizes currently available geologic, geochemical, and isotopic data, and emphasizes results from high-precision geochronology because this technique provides the robust age relationships needed for optimizing ore deposit models and mineral exploration programs. Longstanding genetic paradigms are also questioned for some of the deposits and districts, in order to stimulate additional research on the great diversity of mineralization present in the Belt-Purcell Basin.

sections.heading: The Mesoproterozoic Belt-Purcell Basin
paragraphs: Strata of the Belt-Purcell Basin cover approximately 200,000 km 2  in the northern Rocky Mountains of the United States and Canada (Figs.  1  and  2 ). These strata consist of variably metamorphosed siliciclastic sedimentary rocks (shale, siltstone, argillite), minor carbonate, and local basaltic flows and sills, with a total stratigraphic thickness of 17 to 22 km that on a regional basis includes ~ 7.5 to 12.5 km of unexposed lower units imaged by deep seismic reflection and magnetotelluric profiles (Winston and Link  158 ; Lydon  91 ; Bedrosian and Box  14 ; Lonn et al.  89 ; Hirtz et al.  66 ). Sedimentation in the basin took place from ~ 1480 to ~ 1250 Ma. Major regional stratigraphic units and facies are shown in Fig.  3 . Geologic studies suggest that the lower part of the basin, including strata of the Aldridge Formation of the Purcell Supergroup and equivalent Prichard Formation of the Belt Supergroup, formed in a deep-water, intracontinental rift setting coeval with the emplacement of numerous synsedimentary gabbroic sills, whereas the upper part has shallow-water platform and local non-marine facies. No volcanic rocks are known in the Aldridge or Prichard formations, but two volcaniclastic units up to 22 m thick occur locally in the middle Aldridge Formation (Höy et al.  71 ,  72 ).

Fig. 1 Distribution of the Belt-Purcell Basin in the United States and Canada showing major ore deposits and minor deposits and occurrences discussed in text. Not shown are the small stratabound North Star Pb–Zn–Ag deposit and small Bull River Cu–Ag–Au vein deposit, respectively 3 km south and 60 km southeast of the Sullivan deposit; for other deposits, prospects, and occurrences in southeastern British Columbia, see text and information in Höy et al. ( 72 ), Anderson ( 5 ), PJX Resources Inc. ( 106 ), and Eagle Plains Resources ( 40 ). A, B, C, and D are locations of stratigraphic columns shown in Fig.  2 . Modified from Box et al. ( 21 )

Fig. 2 Stratigraphic divisions of Belt and Purcell supergroups showing generalized locations of major mineral deposits. Lemhi Group and Apple Creek Formation (not shown) are considered broadly correlative to strata of the Missoula Group (see text). Notes: Garnet Range is Garnet Range Formation; Middle Belt Carbonate is carbonate of middle part of Belt Supergroup; Chamberlain is Chamberlain Shale; Neihart is Neihart Quartzite; Newland is Newland Formation; LaHood is LaHood Formation; Fm, formation. Locations of columns  A ,  B ,  C , and  D  are shown in Fig.  1 . Modified from Lydon ( 91 )

Fig. 3 Outcrop area of Belt and Purcell supergroups showing tourmalinite occurrences within siliciclastic strata of Aldridge and Prichard formations and coextensive tholeiitic Moyie gabbroic sills. Isoliths are for outcropping Moyie sills in uppermost part of Lower Aldridge and Middle Aldridge Formation, but do not reflect volume of sills seismically imaged in unexposed lower part of rift-fill sequence. Tourmalinite occurrences from Slack ( 126 ) and Höy et al. ( 72 ). Modified from Lydon ( 91 )

Strata in the western half of the Belt-Purcell Basin had western sedimentary sources usually interpreted as Australia-Antarctica based on geochronology and paleogeographic reconstructions (Dalziel  36 ; Ross and Villeneuve  116 ; Halpin et al.  58 ; Armistead et al.  10 ). These sources were subsequently rifted away from Laurentia, first during the demise of supercontinent Columbia (Nuna) in late middle Proterozoic time and again later during the demise of supercontinent Rodinia in the late Neoproterozoic (Box et al.  22 ; Brennan et al.  23 ,  24 ).

Evaporite deposition in the upper parts of the supergroups is suggested by silica pseudomorphs after gypsum crystals and anhydrite nodules (White  155 ), and by numerous occurrences of scapolite (Box et al.  21 ; and references therein). Evidence for evaporites in lower parts of the Belt and Purcell supergroups includes boron isotope data for tourmaline-rich rocks at the Sullivan deposit and elsewhere in the Aldridge and Prichard formations (Jiang et al.  77 ,  78 ), and mass-balance constraints related to the abundance of boron in tourmalinites at the Sullivan deposit (Slack et al.  133 ). Basement rocks, which crop out mainly in central and northern Idaho, comprise Paleoproterozoic and lesser Neoarchean gneiss, schist, and amphibolite (Doughty and Chamberlain  39 ; Vervoort et al.  153 ).

Post-depositional processes that affected Belt-Purcell strata include deformation, metamorphism, and magmatism. Minor folding and greenschist-facies metamorphism (McMechan and Price  98 ) and local bimodal magmatism occurred mainly during the 1379 to 1325 Ma East Kootenay orogeny (Doughty and Chamberlain  38 ,  39 ; Schandl and Davis  121 ; Aleinikoff et al.  2 ; McFarlane  95 ; Bookstrom et al.  20 ). The 1150 to 980 Ma Grenvillian orogeny, where present, produced varying effects from limited recrystallization of rocks and minerals to upper greenschist-facies metamorphism (e.g.Anderson and Davis  7 ; Anderson and Parrish  8 ; Nesheim et al.  101 ; Aleinikoff et al.  2 ). The younger Goat River orogeny, from about 900 to 800 Ma, is recorded locally by uplift, block faulting, and low-grade regional metamorphism (McMechan and Price  98 ). Phanerozoic events produced Paleozoic, Cretaceous, and early Tertiary faults, episodic magmatism, and selected mineral recrystallization (Zirakparvar et al.  162 ; Lund et al.  90 ; Aleinikoff et al.  2 ; Bookstrom et al.  20 ; Saintilan et al.  118 ). Major shortening across the Belt-Purcell Basin, on the order of 200 to 250 km, occurred during the late Mesozoic (Cook et al.  33 ; Price and Sears  108 ; Bedrosian and Box  14 ).

sections.heading: Sullivan stratabound Pb–Zn–Ag deposit
paragraphs: The Sullivan Pb–Zn–Ag deposit in southeastern British Columbia (Fig.  1 ) is arguably the most important single orebody in the Belt and Purcell supergroups in terms of amount of contained metal. From 1909 to closure in 2001, the Sullivan mine produced 149.7 Mt of ore at an average grade of 5.95% Pb, 5.49% Zn, and 69.6 g/t Ag (Slack et al.  133  and references therein), equivalent to 8.91 Mt of Pb, 8.22 Mt of Zn, and 10,419 t of Ag; appreciable tin (9700 t) was also produced. Regionally, the deposit is contained within siliciclastic metasedimentary rocks of the Aldridge Formation in an area with a large (~ 800 m) thickness of coeval tholeiitic gabbro sills (Fig.  3 ). The mostly stratiform sulfide ores are hosted in argillite and siltite at the top of the lower Aldridge Formation (Hamilton et al.  59 ; Lydon  91 ). The nearby North Star deposit, 3 km south of the Sullivan mine, is a stratiform sulfide lens at the same stratigraphic level, with a small production of only 61,000 t but a very high average grade of 35.5% Pb, 6.12% Zn, and 673 g/t Ag; between Sullivan and North Star is the discordant Stemwinder deposit, a small sulfide-rich vent complex with production + reserves of 150,000 t at an average grade of 3.1% Pb, 16.6% Zn, and 82 g/t Ag (Lydon  91 ).

Stratiform Pb–Zn–Ag ores and a discordant massive pyrrhotite body at the Sullivan deposit (Fig.  4 ) are underlain by a ~ 450-m-thick tourmalinite alteration zone cut by gabbroic sills and dikes, with an overlying albite-chlorite-pyrite alteration zone and a peripheral muscovite alteration zone (Turner et al.  148 ; Lydon  91 ). U–Pb zircon ages for the footwall gabbroic sill and three other Moyie sills within the lower Aldridge Formation are 1468 ± 3 Ma (Anderson and Parrish  8 ; Schandl and Davis  121 ). The tourmalinite zone and massive pyrrhotite body are considered part of a large hydrothermal vent complex. Localization of the Sullivan deposit is by a north-trending sedimentary graben and large (7 × 3 km) seafloor mud volcano, the latter recorded by a discordant and concordant unit composed of pebble fragmental rock and conglomerate (Turner et al.  149 ; Ransom and Lydon  110 ). The age of Pb–Zn–Ag mineralization is constrained broadly by a Sm–Nd isochron date of 1451 ± 46 on carbonate gangue in the bedded ores (Jiang et al.  79 ) and more precisely by a laser-ablation ICP-MS U–Pb date of 1475 ± 4 Ma on cassiterite in paragenetically late veins (Slack et al.  133 ). Geochronological studies of altered rocks and minerals (titanite, polycrase, cassiterite) by Pb–Pb and U–Pb methods document mineral recrystallization and dissolution-reprecipitation at 1373 ± 5, 1328 ± 4, 1325 ± 21, 1076 ± 77, and 996 ± 9 Ma during the East Kootenay and Grenvillian orogenies (Schandl and Davis  121 ; Jiang et al.  79 ; Slack et al.  132 ). Lead isotope data suggest that the lead in the deposit is derived from clastic metasedimentary rocks of the lower Aldridge Formation with a possible contribution from underlying basement rocks (Beaudoin  12 ,  13 ).
Fig. 4 Geologic cross section of the Sullivan Pb–Zn–Ag deposit in southeastern British Columbia; megabreccia and pebble fragmental unit represent a mud volcano deposit. Modified from Lydon ( 91 )

A three-stage genetic model for mineralization by Lydon ( 91 ) involves (1) synsedimentary mud volcano formation linked to gabbroic sill emplacement, followed by vertical transport of fluid + gas + sediment; (2) tourmalinite formation by boron metasomatism of aluminous sediments, at temperatures of 250° to 300 °C (Seal et al.  123 ; Taylor et al.  145 ; Slack  129 ); and (3) Pb–Zn–Ag mineralization via seafloor venting of a metalliferous brine having temperatures up to 215 °C (Taylor et al.  145 ). In the shallow footwall, tourmalinites and associated Mn-rich coticules (garnet-quartz rocks) with pyrrhotite, and some tourmalinites in the hanging wall, may have formed by exhalative processes (Slack et al.  131 ; Slack  129 ). Discordant massive pyrrhotite zones that cut the bedded ores and altered rocks in the hanging wall (tourmalinite, albite-chlorite-pyrite) reflect post-ore hydrothermal processes (Conly et al.  31 ). The overlap of ore mineral, gangue, and mafic intrusive ages provide strong evidence for mineralization occurring during the early rift stage of the Belt-Purcell Basin, coeval with the broadly synsedimentary emplacement of tholeiitic gabbro sills in the footwall of the deposit (see Lydon  91 ). Strontium and Nd isotope data for the sulfide ores and altered wall rocks suggest sources of these metals from three sources: (1) underlying gabbroic sills, (2) clastic sediments of the lower Aldridge Formation, and (2) deeper basement rocks of Paleoproterozoic and possibly Archean age (Slack et al.  130 ). Lead isotope values for galena from the deposit define a predominant array that reflects mixing between a sedimentary source in the lower Aldridge Formation and an older source likely from unexposed Precambrian basement rocks (Beaudoin  12 ,  13 ).

Based on the presence of fine laminations of sphalerite and galena that characterize the bedded ores, most workers have invoked a wholly syngenetic origin for the Pb–Zn–Ag mineralization (e.g., Hamilton et al.  59 ; Lydon  91 ). This interpretation is supported by detailed sulfur and carbon isotope values of the bedded ores (pyrrhotite, sphalerite, galena, pyrite, carbonate) that are attributed to deposition by both thermochemical and biogenic sulfate reduction in a brine pool (Taylor  143 ). However, occurrences of bedded dolomite in the ores reported by Taylor and Beaudoin ( 144 ) suggest that local zones within the sulfide deposit formed by subseafloor replacement of carbonate sediments. A major outstanding question is whether a majority of the stratiform Pb–Zn–Ag ores at the Sullivan deposit reflects this type of epigenetic mineralization.

sections.heading: Coeur d’Alene district Ag–Pb–Zn–(Cu) veins
paragraphs: Significant quantities of metal have been mined from the Ag–Pb–Zn–(Cu) veins of the Coeur d’Alene district in northern Idaho (Fig.  1 ). Total production from 1884 to 2023 from > 90 mines is more than 120 Mt of ore including 39,542 t Ag, 7.89 Mt Pb, 3.09 Mt Zn, and 0.19 Mt Cu (Gillerman  51 ; V.S. Gillerman, Idaho Geological Survey, written communication 2025). Minor amounts of As and Sb have also been produced as byproducts. Metal grades among the many mines of the district vary greatly due to different proportions of ore minerals, such as dominant Pb and Zn in some veins vs. abundant Ag or Sb in others, hence specifying typical grades would be misleading.

Veins of the district extend from the upper part of the Prichard Formation to the lower part of the Wallace Formation of the Belt Supergroup; most veins are localized in quartzite of the Revett Formation of the Belt Supergroup (e.g., Fryklund  44 ; Mauk and White  93 ). Individual veins range in width from a few centimeters to several meters or more, and in length typically more than 300 m and vertically for over 1000 m, and in a few cases, at least 2500 m (Fryklund  44 ). Many of the veins cut folded host rocks. Mineral assemblages vary from quartz + siderite + galena + sphalerite, to quartz + siderite + argentiferous tetrahedrite, to quartz + carbonate. The Pb–Zn veins are reportedly the oldest in the paragenetic sequence. A reconstruction of vein assemblages in the region by Hofstra et al. ( 67 ) shows that the Ag-rich veins with abundant tetrahedrite tend to occur at shallow structural levels whereas Pb–Zn veins are at intermediate depths and Sb-rich but Ag-poor veins (stibnite + quartz ± sulfides) occur at the deepest structural levels (Fig.  5 ). Fluid inclusion studies indicate that ore deposition in the veins occurred at temperatures of 250° to 300 °C and pressures above 1 kbar (Leach et al.  86 ). Importantly, two distinct trends of data are shown by Pb-isotope values in the district, one a less-radiogenic array for galena from the Zn- and Pb-rich veins that records a Proterozoic (1.0 Ga) source for the Pb, and the other a more radiogenic array for tetrahedrite and siderite from the Ag-rich veins and for stibnite from the Sb-rich but Ag-poor veins that reflects a Late Cretaceous to early Tertiary source (Leach et al.  87 ).

Fig. 5 Schematic cross section of Coeur d’Alene Ag–Pb–Zn–(Cu) district in northern Idaho showing diverse metal assemblages in veins at different stratigraphic and structural levels. Distribution of the different vein types as shown does not imply a paragenetic or genetic relationship among them. Fm, formation. Modified from Hofstra et al. ( 67 )

A variety of geochronological and fluid inclusion data suggest that most of the vein mineralization in the district occurred during the Proterozoic although interpretations vary from very early, post-depositional mineralization in the Mesoproterozoic to late Mesozoic mineralization. Very early mineralization is suggested by dating of siderite samples from ore-bearing veins that yield a Sm–Nd isochron age of 1511 ± 45 Ma and carbonates from barren veins with a broadly coeval Pb–Pb isochron age of 1523 ± 41 Ma (Ramos and Rosenberg  109 ); these ages barely overlap, within uncertainty, the depositional age of the host Revett Formation (1480 − 1450 Ma), thus permitting a model of vein opening and filling during diagenesis. The suggestion by Ramos and Rosenberg ( 109 ) that these ages reflect mineralization during a pre-1460 Ma metamorphic event is inconsistent with generally accepted ages of Belt Supergroup strata. Much younger are cores of xenotime crystals from a barren quartz-carbonate vein that yielded a laser-ablation U–Pb age of 1420 ± 90 Ma (Ramos and Rosenberg  109 ), and a brannerite-bearing jasperoid vein with a U–Pb concordia age of 1344 ± 42 Ma (Zartman and Smith  160 ). A more direct Mesoproterozoic link to ore mineralization is provided by a Re–Os isochron date of 1327 ± 32 Ma on arsenopyrite intergrown with siderite and locally tetrahedrite from the Galena mine (Arkadakskiy et al.  9 ; S. Arkadakskiy and R.A. Creaser, University of Alberta, written communication 2025), consistent with deposition from metamorphic fluids during the 1379 to 1325 Ma East Kootenay orogeny.  40 Ar/ 39 Ar plateau ages of ≥ 1018 Ma obtained on sericite from a Zn–Pb–Ag vein (Leach et al.  87 ) and ≥ 1014 Ma on sericite from a calcite-rich vein (Rosenberg and Larson  115 ) are permissive for linking mineralization to the Grenvillian orogeny; younger  40 Ar/ 39 Ar plateau ages of 970.6 ± 37.3 and 929.3 ± 30.4 Ma for fluorphlogopite from two quartz-ankerite veins (Rosenberg and Larson  115 ) may reflect elevated temperatures during the waning stages of that orogeny. A metamorphogenic origin for the veins of the Coeur d’Alene district is further supported by fluid inclusion studies of Leach et al. ( 86 ) and Landis and Hofstra ( 84 ) that show gas compositions of primary inclusions in quartz vary from organic-rich (CH 4  mainly) in the older Zn-rich veins to CO 2 -rich in the younger Ag-rich (also W and Sb) veins. These data were interpreted to record mineral precipitation from fluids characteristic of devolatilization processes in mid-crustal metamorphic settings, and not from shallow granitic plutons like those of the Late Cretaceous-early Tertiary Idaho Batholith as proposed by Eaton et al. ( 42 ) on the basis of stable isotope and Sr isotope data for the veins.

Other dating and isotope studies have yielded much younger ages. Samples of vein sericite from the Sunshine and Baychief mines have  40 Ar/ 39 Ar plateau ages of 87 to 64 Ma, suggesting a genetic link to emplacement of the Idaho Batholith (e.g., Leach et al.  86 ,  87 ). However, C and O isotope data for siderite with δ 18 O values of less than 16‰ suggest deposition at both high temperatures and high pressures, from metamorphic fluids. Highly radiogenic Sr isotope values of carbonate gangue minerals in the veins require an old source for the Sr at the time of mineralization such as strata of the Belt Supergroup for Mesozoic mineralization (Fleck et al.  43 ), or underlying Archean rocks for Mesoproterozoic mineralization (Rosenberg and Larson  115 ). Oxygen and hydrogen isotope values of quartz and inclusion fluids from one Ag-rich vein suggest mineralization occurred from a mixture of metamorphic fluids and meteoric waters (Constantopoulos and Larson  32 ).

An integrated assessment by Leach et al. ( 87 ) of geologic, geochemical, and geochronological, and Pb-isotope data proposed that the Zn- and Pb-rich veins formed in the Proterozoic, whereas the Ag- and Sb-rich veins formed in the Late Cretaceous to early Tertiary. Collectively, these results provide compelling evidence for multiple periods of vein mineralization in the Coeur d’Alene district over a protracted period of approximately 1 b.y. Additional high-precision geochronology in the district could help to better refine the ages of vein mineralization, particularly evaluating the relative proportion of ore deposition during the East Kootenay vs. Grenvillian orogenies.

sections.heading: Stratabound Cu–Co–Au–(Bi–Y–REE) deposits of the Idaho cobalt belt
paragraphs: Mineral deposits of the Idaho cobalt belt (Figs.  1  and  6 ) are noteworthy for containing a distinctive metal assemblage of Cu–Co with local concentrations of Au, Bi, Ni, Y, and REE (Slack  127 ,  128 ). Past production + resources are ~ 17 Mt at an average grade of 0.74% Co, 1.4% Cu, and 1.0 g/t Au (Bookstrom et al.  21 ; Bookstrom and Box  18 ). Reconnaissance whole-rock analyses of Co-rich ore samples show up to 9.16 wt % Bi, up to 0.83 wt % Y, up to 2.56 wt % ΣREE oxides, up to 6,780 ppm Ni, and in a few deposits up to 1,180 ppm Be, up to 124 ppm U, and up to 133 ppm Sn; Zn and Pb contents are uniformly low at ≤ 821 and ≤ 61 ppm, respectively (Slack  128 ). Deposits in the 60-km-long, northwest-trending belt form stratabound lenses and discordant structures within interbedded argillite and siltite of the Apple Creek Formation of the Lemhi Group. This formation has a maximum age of ~ 1.41 Ga based on U–Pb dates on detrital zircons, suggesting correlation with strata of the Mount Shields or Bonner formations of the Missoula Group (Aleinikoff et al.  2 ; Link et al.  88 ) (Fig.  2 ); correlation with the younger Garnet Range Formation of the Missoula Group is also possible (Gaschnig et al.  49 ). Most of the stratabound deposits and their enclosing alteration zones are folded, and some are strongly sheared. In the Blackbird district, most of the eight known stratabound deposits are less than a few meters wide and several hundred meters long, but some are as much as 25 m wide and 1000 m long (Vhay  154 ; Bookstrom et al.  20 ). Cobaltite, chalcopyrite, and gold in the stratabound deposits occur with minor amounts of xenotime, monazite, and allanite locally; cobaltite textures range from fine-grained disseminations to granoblastic aggregates. Gangue minerals include predominant quartz, chlorite, tourmaline, and biotite, with generally minor amounts of muscovite, garnet, chloritoid, siderite, fluorapatite, and/or magnetite (Slack  128 ; Bookstrom et al.  20 ).
Fig. 6 Simplified geologic map of Idaho cobalt belt showing principal mineral deposits and occurrences. Modified from Bookstrom and Box ( 18 )

The stratabound deposits are typically enclosed by conformable alteration zones typically several meters thick that contain ≥ 75 vol % biotite (Fig.  7 ; Bookstrom et al.  20 ). Other constituents of these distinctive biotite-rich rocks, termed “biotitite”, include tourmaline and quartz, local cobaltite, and sparse allanite and chalcopyrite. The biotitites were interpreted by Nash and Hahn ( 100 ) as alkaline mafic tuffs, which served as the basis of their volcanogenic massive sulfide (VMS) model for mineralization in the district. However, trace element systematics of the biotitites suggest instead that these rocks represent hydrothermally altered siliciclastic sediments (Bookstrom et al.  20 ). Mafic dikes of varying composition cut the stratabound deposits and are likely of early Paleozoic age based on geochemical similarity to 530 to 485 Ma mafic dikes elsewhere in the region (Bookstrom et al.  20  and references therein).

Fig. 7 Generalized geologic map of Blackbird Co–Cu–Au district showing stratabound and discordant sulfide deposits and related biotite-rich alteration zones. Blue line outlines Blacktail mine open pit. Stippled pattern represents rocks at and above garnet isograd (Grt ± Cld ± Crd); Grt = garnet, Cld = chloritoid, Crd = cordierite. Modified from Slack ( 128 ) after Bookstrom et al. ( 19 )

Discordant mineralized structures mainly comprise quartz-sulfide veins and quartz-tourmaline-cobaltite breccias (Bookstrom et al.  20 ). The former, which cut the stratabound deposits and younger mafic dikes, consist of quartz, pyrite, pyrrhotite, and minor chalcopyrite, arsenopyrite, and siderite. The quartz-tourmaline-cobaltite breccias form dikes and pipes within quartzite host rocks, both unmineralized and mineralized. Cobaltite, together with minor chalcopyrite, vary in texture from veinlets and stockworks to small lenses composed of fine-grained, highly sheared cobaltite. In addition to Co, whole-rock analyses show very high contents of Au, Ni, U, Y, and HREE in a few samples, (Slack  128 ; Appendix 1), thus suggesting a genetic link to the stratabound deposits.

Radiogenic and stable isotope studies provide additional insights into the multielement mineralization of the district. Pb-isotope values for pyrite, chalcopyrite, pyrrhotite, and cobaltite suggest a lead source from old upper crustal rocks such as the clastic metasediments of the host Apple Creek Formation, but not from the nearby Mesoproterozoic granites (Panneerselvam et al.  104 ). Sulfur isotope values for cobaltite show a narrow range from 6.4 to 8.9‰, suggesting a partly sedimentary source for the sulfur; overall, O and H isotope data for the Co–Cu–Au deposits preclude modified seawater as the predominant fluid component and thus argue against VMS (or sedimentary-exhalative) origins and instead point to deep-seated metamorphic or less-likely magmatic processes of mineralization (Johnson et al.  80 ). Based on in situ SIMS B-isotope values of tourmaline in the deposits, calculated fluid values (at an inferred temperature of 300 °C) range from − 3 to 7‰, the isotopically light boron attributed to derivation from clastic sediments in the footwall of the deposits, and the isotopically heavy boron from marine carbonates and/or B-bearing evaporites (Trumbull et al.  147 ). A model that involves evaporites in the Co–Cu–Au mineralization is supported by occurrences of Na- and Cl-rich (marialitic) scapolite in some of the biotite-rich altered rocks distal from the deposits and in the host metasedimentary strata regionally (Nash and Connor  99 ; Tysdal and Desborough  150 ; Bookstrom et al.  20 ), and by Na, Cl, and Br ratios of fluid inclusion extracts from gangue quartz that contain a hypersaline population produced by the evaporation of seawater beyond halite saturation (Landis and Hofstra  85 ). Determining halogen ratios in district scapolite holds promise for identifying halite dissolution and residual bittern brine sources with related applications to the ore-forming fluids in the Idaho cobalt belt. The recent study by Rein et al. ( 113 ) determined Cl/Br ratios in scapolite from this belt, arguing for a predominant residual bittern brine component and a postore fluid timing for scapolite formation, but their reported U–Pb titanite age of 1231 ± 18 Ma for a scapolite-bearing outcrop is not clearly meaningful for the age of the scapolite because no textural relationship is shown between this mineral and the dated titanite.

Genetic models for the mineralization range widely from syngenetic Besshi-type VMS (Earhart  41 ; Nash and Hahn  100 ), to sedimentary-exhalative (Nold  102 ; Bending and Scales  15 ), to iron oxide-copper-gold (IOCG) related to Mesoproterozoic granite magmatism (Slack  128 ), to epigenetic during Cretaceous metamorphism (Lund et al.  90 ). The IOCG model is supported by (1) intergrowths of cobaltite with xenotime, dated at 1370 ± 4 Ma (SHRIMP U–Pb; Aleinikoff et al.  2 ) and 1349 ± 76 Ma (Re–Os; Saintilan et al.  118 ), coeval with the SHRIMP U–Pb age of 1377 ± 4 Ma obtained for zircon from a nearby megacrystic granite (Aleinikoff et al.  2 ); (2) gas geochemical data for saline fluid inclusions in quartz gangue of the Co-rich deposits that require a magmatic component (Landis and Hofstra  85 ); (3) the presence of Be-rich gadolinite locally in the ores and Be-bearing pegmatites in the margin of the 1377 Ma pluton (Slack  128 ); (4) occurrences of magnetite within and near the main Co–Cu–Au deposits and of extensive lenses of pyrite-rich magnetite in the Iron Creek area (Fig.  6 ; Slack  128 ; Bookstrom et al.  20 ; Holley et al.  68 ); and (5) trace-element data for magnetite from samples of Cu–Co-related ore that mainly plot in the IOCG field on a Ti + V vs. Al + Mn discriminant diagram (Gillerman et al.  54 ). An IOCG model is also consistent with formation of the Co and Be–Y–REE mineralization by one Mesoproterozoic hydrothermal system, coeval with bimodal magmatism during the early stage of the 1379 to 1325 Ma East Kootenay orogeny. Some xenotime grains in Co-rich samples have SHRIMP U–Pb ages of 1315 to 1270 Ma and ~ 1050 Ma, recording episodic dissolution and reprecipitation of this mineral during the waning stages of this orogeny and the younger 1150 to 980 Ma Grenvillian orogeny (Aleinikoff et al.  2 ; Slack  128 ). However, it is likely that most of the Cu, Au, and Bi was introduced during Cretaceous metamorphism based on cross-cutting textural relationships in the deposits (Lund et al.  90 ; Bookstrom et al.  20 ) and on the statistical separation via factor analysis of Cu from Co and As in whole-rock analyses of mineralized samples (Slack  128 ). Effects of Cretaceous metamorphism on the deposits are well documented by SHRIMP U–Pb ages for monazite in cobaltite-rich ore samples (~ 110 and ~ 92 Ma; Aleinikoff et al.  2 ) and by a  40 Ar/ 39 Ar isochron age of 82.9 ± 1.1 Ma for muscovite in a late quartz vein (Lund et al.  90 ). A more complex model for the origin of the Iron Creek deposits by Zaronikola et al. ( 159 ), based on Cu isotopes and Co concentrations in pyrite, posits the introduction of Co into local siliciclastic strata during a Mesoproterozoic sedimentary-exhalative process, followed by remobilization of the original pyrite by CO 2 -rich metamorphic fluids during the Mesoproterozoic East Kootenay and Grenvillian orogenies, and by the Late Jurassic to Late Cretaceous Cordilleran orogeny.

An untested possibility, albeit unlikely to explain all occurrences, involves the introduction of major metal concentrations into the district (Fe, Co, Cu, Au, Ni, Bi, Be, Y, REE) during the middle Mesoproterozoic, followed by greenschist-facies metamorphic processes during the Grenvillian orogeny and later orogeny of the Cretaceous Period. This process would selectively transport, via mechanical and fluid-based mobilization, Cu, Bi, and Au from minerals like chalcopyrite, pyrrhotite, and gold into veins and other discordant structures (see Craw  34 ; Marshall and Spry  92 ; Tomkins  146 ). In contrast, Fe, Ni, Co, Be, Y, and REE that mainly reside in more mechanically and chemically resistant minerals like magnetite, pyrite, cobaltite, gadolinite, and xenotime were largely retained in primary stratabound lenses (cf. Rasmussen et al.  112 ; de Araujo et al.  37 ).

sections.heading: Spar Lake and related large stratabound sediment-hosted Cu–Ag deposits
paragraphs: Large stratabound sediment-hosted Cu–Ag deposits at Spar Lake in western Montana and similar deposits in this region (Rock Creek, Montanore) occur in quartzite of the Revett Formation of the Ravalli Group (Figs.  1  and  8 ). Production from the Spar Lake (formerly Troy) mine, from 1981 to 2012, totals 39.2 Mt of ore at an average grade of 0.62% Cu and 42 g/t Ag; proven + probable reserves as of 2012 were 11.1 Mt at 0.39% Cu and 31.4 g/t Ag (Revett Minerals, Inc.  114 ). The Spar Lake mine closed permanently in 2015. Inferred resources for the unmined Rock Creek and Montanore (formerly Libby) deposits are 100.0 Mt at 0.70% Cu and 42 g/t Ag, and 112.2 Mt at 0.70% Cu and 45 g/t Ag, respectively (Hecla Mining Company  64 ). These deposits consist of disseminations of bornite, digenite, chalcocite, and native silver, together with minor pyrite, chalcopyrite, and galena in a gangue of calcite, chlorite, and ankerite; hematite and clay are principal alteration phases in wall rocks (Hayes et al.  63 ). Ore zones range stratigraphically up to tens of meters thick; low-grade mineralized zones are as much as 480 m thick (Boleneus et al.  16 ). At the Spar Lake deposit, mineral zoning is expressed by assemblages of pyrite-calcite, galena-calcite, chalcopyrite-calcite, bornite-calcite, chalcocite-chlorite, and chalcopyrite-ankerite that are discordant to bedding at low angles; the bornite-calcite and chalcocite-chlorite zones generally have the highest ore grades of > 0.4% Cu and > 1 oz/t Ag (Hayes and Einaudi  61 ). Sulfur isotope geothermometry of paired sulfide minerals suggest formational temperatures of 50 to 115 °C (Hayes et al.  62 ). A broadly accepted genetic model for the deposits involves diagenetic mineralization in which copper and silver minerals form cements and replace clasts and paragenetically early phases (carbonate, pyrite) in a reaction zone between oxidized metalliferous brine and sour H 2 S-bearing natural gas (e.g., Hayes and Einaudi  61 ; Hayes et al.  63 ). However, the discovery by P. Perelló and D. Anderson of fracture- and bedding-controlled epigenetic mineralization and alteration underground and in drill cores from the high-grade parts of the Spar Lake and Montanore deposits (Fig.  9 ) argues against a wholly diagenetic model for the Cu–Ag mineralization there. Geochronological studies have reported a Mesoproterozoic SHRIMP U–Pb date of 1409 ± 8 Ma for xenotime overgrowths on zircon from the Spar Lake deposit (Aleinikoff et al.  1 ), but this xenotime is not texturally associated with the Cu–Ag mineralization and thus may only reflect barren diagenetic fluid flow unrelated to ore formation. More relevant is a 1043 ± 6 Ma Re–Os date on molybdenite intergrown with bornite and chalcocite from a stratabound Cu–Ag prospect in the Creston Formation (correlative with the Revett Formation) of the Belt and Purcell supergroups, recording mineralization during the Grenvillian orogeny (Perelló et al.  105 ). A recent Re–Os isochron date of 253 ± 27 Ma obtained on bornite from the Rock Creek deposit suggests reworking of older mineralization and the possibility of a second ore-forming event in the Permian (Saintilan and Creaser  117 ). The Grenvillian Re–Os date on the molybdenite, which is unlikely to reflect isotopic resetting of diagenetic mineralization by metamorphism (e.g., Stein et al.  141 ), is clearly incompatible with a wholly diagenetic model for Cu–Ag mineralization in the Creston Formation, as are the Christmas-tree structures of epigenetic sulfides and gangue minerals that occur within the Revett Formation (Fig.  9 ). These results thus prompt several important questions: (1) Did only parts of the Cu–Ag deposits form during diagenesis? (2) Could the well-documented disseminated textures and sulfide-alteration zonations reflect epigenetic and not diagenetic mineralization? (3) If the copper sulfides formed mainly during diagenesis and were later remobilized by orogenic-related metamorphism, how can the ore mineralogy and paragenetic relationships remain unchanged? (P. Perelló, Santiago, Chile, written communication 2025). These questions underscore how additional research—especially high-precision geochronology supported by careful paragenetic studies—can help to better constrain genetic models and improve exploration programs for stratabound Cu–Ag deposits in strata of the Belt-Purcell Basin of western Montana and southeastern British Columbia.

Spar Lake Cu–Ag deposit (not shown) is within the upper member of the Revett Formation. m, meters above sea level. Modified from Saintilan and Creaser ( 117 )

sections.heading: Black Butte stratiform Cu–Co–Ag deposits
paragraphs: The unmined Black Butte (formerly Sheep Creek) Cu–Co–Ag deposit occurs in the Helena embayment of western Montana (Fig.  1 ). This deposit consists of two principal mineralized lenses, the upper and lower zones of the Johnny Lee deposit (Fig.  10 ) that have combined proven + probable reserves of 9.5 Mt at an average grade of 2.9% Cu and measured + indicated resources of 18.9 Mt at an average grade of 2.4% Cu (Sandfire Resources America, Inc.  120 ). Previously, Tintina Resources, Inc. delineated for the upper zone an inferred resource of 8.48 Mt at an average grade of 2.96% Cu, 0.12% Co, and 16.4 g/t Ag (Graham et al.  57 ). The Lowry deposit, ~ 3 km to the southeast, has measured + indicated resources of 6.6 Mt at an average grade of 2.4% Cu (Sandfire Resources America, Inc.  120 ), for a total tonnage for the combined Black Butte and Lowry deposits of ~ 15 Mt. The different mineralized zones are contained in a local fault-controlled graben, within dolomitic shale, debris-flow conglomerate, and other sedimentary facies of the Newland Formation in the lower part of the Belt Supergroup (Zieg et al.  161 ; Graham et al.  57 ).

Fig. 10 Geologic cross section of Strawberry Main portion of Black Butte (formerly Sheep Creek) Cu–Co–Ag deposit in western Montana showing debris flows, multiple stratabound pyritic (± chalcopyrite ± barite) lenses, and selected drill holes. LSZ, Lower Sulfide Zone. Modified from Graham et al. ( 57 )

The stratiform sulfide zones contain chalcopyrite, siegenite, and tennantite that replace cobaltiferous pyrite, carbonate, and barite (Graham et al.  57 ; White et al.  157 ). Based on proximity of the fault zone, Schieber ( 122 ) proposed a model of epigenetic mineralization related to a hypothesized early Tertiary igneous intrusion. An older synsedimentary to diagenetic origin is supported by the geometry of the mineralized zones and related textures (Graham et al.  57 ), and by the occurrence of pyrite-walled tube structures (Present et al.  107 ). A chalcopyrite Re–Os isochron age of 1488 ± 34 Ma provides compelling evidence for mineralization occurring broadly during sedimentation and diagenesis (Saintilan et al.  119 ), the former setting likely aiding sulfide formation by the presence of H 2 S-bearing suboxic or euxinic bottom waters (Slotznick et al.  134 ).

sections.heading: Th–REE–(Cu) veins
paragraphs: The Lemhi Pass district in eastern Idaho and westernmost Montana (Fig.  1 ) comprises numerous veins of thorite and Nd-rich monazite with minor chalcopyrite and bornite, and sparse molybdenite, in a gangue of quartz, hematite, apatite, feldspar, and local biotite (Anderson  4 ; Sharp and Cavender  124 ; Staatz et al.  139 ; Staatz  138 ; Gillerman et al.  53 ). Host rocks to the veins are clastic metasedimentary rocks of the Mesoproterozoic Lemhi Group that, on the basis of U–Pb detrital zircon ages, is correlative with strata of the Missoula Group of the Belt Supergroup. This district reportedly has the largest Th resource known in the United States (Van Gosen et al.  152 ), but no documented reserves or resources are published. Smaller Th–REE–(Cu) deposits, to the northwest in the Diamond Creek and Mineral Hill districts, are spatially associated with carbonatite dikes (Anderson  3 ). All of these deposits are deformed and metamorphosed. Mesoproterozoic ages were obtained by Re–Os dating of molybdenite (1055 ± 4 Ma) and by U–Pb of monazite cores (~ 1100 Ma), whereas predominantly Paleozoic Th–U–Pb ages are recorded by monazite rims (400 − 200 Ma) and thorite cores (370 − 330 Ma) (Gillerman et al.  52 ). Fluid inclusion microthermometry and zirconium-in-rutile geothermometry by May and Appold ( 94 ) suggest that vein formation occurred at high temperatures of 470° to 540° C and pressures of 4.9 to 9.8 kbars, by very saline fluids with high F concentrations. These data, together with the geochronological results (especially U–Pb and Re–Os dates), provide strong evidence for Th–REE–(Cu) mineralization occurring at middle to lower crustal depths during the Grenvillian orogeny, followed by hydrothermal overprinting during one or more Devonian to Carboniferous magmatic and/or tectonic events. The model of Gillerman et al. ( 55 ) emphasizes only a younger, Devonian to Mississippian mineralizing event (Fig.  11 ). However, given characteristic dissolution and reprecipitation of REE in monazite and thorite during metamorphism (e.g.Rasmussen and Muhling  111 ; Slack et al.  132 ; Aleinikoff et al.  1 ,  2 ), it is unclear how much, if any, new Th–REE–(Cu) was introduced into these deposits during the Paleozoic.

Fig. 11 Schematic model for formation of Th–REE–(Cu) veins in Lemhi Pass district, Idaho and Montana, showing inferred hydrothermal fluid flow during Devonian to Mississippian time, in which fluids leach phosphatic Fe-Mn nodules in sedimentary strata for distal precipitation of Th and REE phosphates. Yl, Mesoproterozoic clastic metasedimentary rocks of Lemhi Group; Yag, Mesoproterozoic augen gneiss/granite; Ꞓmi, Cambrian mafic dikes; Ꞓsy, Cambrian syenite; OꞒi, Ordovician to Cambrian plutons. Blue arrows are schematic hydrothermal fluid circulation paths. Modified from Gillerman et al. ( 55 )

Several deposits of rare metals occur outside of the Lemhi Pass district. Prominent among these are the Th–REE veins at the Hall Mountain deposit in northernmost Idaho that occur within or adjacent to gabbroic sills in the Prichard Formation (Fig.  1 ; Staatz  137 ). These veins, locally brecciated, are up to 210 m long and up to 4 m wide. Thorite is the principal ore mineral, accompanied by minor pyrite, chalcopyrite, pyrrhotite, allanite, and kainosite-(Y), and with rare monazite, in a gangue composed of quartz with local calcite and fluorite (Staatz  137 ; Staatz et al.  140 ).

sections.heading: Stratabound Pb–Zn–Ag
paragraphs: Many small stratabound Pb–Zn–Ag deposits and prospects occur in the lower part of the Purcell Supergroup in southeastern British Columbia up to tens of kilometers from the Sullivan deposit (Fig.  1 ; Höy et al.  72 ). Within the lower and middle Aldridge Formation, most deposits and prospects are hosted by, or spatially associated with, variably fragmental sedimentary rocks interpreted as mud volcano deposits (Anderson and Höy  6 ; Kennedy and Höy  83 ). These mud volcano deposits range from stratabound lenses to steeply dipping structures, all of which likely reflect diagenetic dewatering of the sedimentary pile. Related tourmaline concentrations, including tourmalinites, also vary in geometry and occur in both the Aldridge and Prichard formations (Beaty et al.  11 ; Slack  126 ; Höy et al.  72 ). All of the known sulfide deposits outside of the Sullivan corridor are at or above strata of the middle Aldridge Formation (Lydon  91 ). The Fors prospect comprises stratiform massive sulfide lenses with associated disseminations and veins (Britton and Pighin  26 ). The K-9 prospect, above the Aldridge Formation in the Creston Formation, contains vein and replacement-style Cu–Ag–Pb–Zn mineralization (Eagle Plains Resources  40 ). Other significant sulfide prospects and occurrences include Pakk, CanAm, Star, and Vulcan (Höy et al.  72 ; Anderson  5 ; Eagle Plains Resources  40 ).

East of the Sullivan mine the Kootenay King deposit (Fig.  1 ) produced 13,260 t of ore at an average grade of 15.6% Zn, 5.35% Pb, 67.0 g/t Ag, and minor Au (Lydon  91 ). This stratiform deposit is within quartzite and argillite in the upper part of the lower Aldridge Formation and has strong muscovite alteration in wall rocks (Höy  69 ; Höy et al.  72 ). The Dewdney Trail prospects, 6 to 8 km to the north in the Estella mine area (Fig.  1 ), contain stratiform Pb–Zn–Ag mineralization associated with fragmental rocks and tourmalinites like at the Sullivan deposit (PJX Resources, Inc.  106 ).

In western Montana, the Soap Gulch prospect (Fig.  1 ) forms a stratiform sulfide lens in argillite and dolostone of the LaHood Formation of the Belt Supergroup (Gammons et al.  47 ). Exploration there by numerous companies has identified locally high concentrations of Zn, Cu, Co, and Au (Bolt Metals Corporation  17 ).

sections.heading: Sediment-hosted stratabound Cu–Ag
paragraphs: Sediment-hosted stratabound Cu–Ag prospects are known in several parts of southeastern British Columbia (Hartlaub et al.  60 ; Perelló et al.  105 ). These prospects are geologically and mineralogically similar to the large deposits (Spar Lake, Rock Creek, Montanore) in western Montana. Chalcopyrite, bornite, and chalcocite form bedding-parallel disseminations in quartzite and siltite of the Creston Formation, which is stratigraphically equivalent to the Revett Formation that hosts the deposits in western Montana (Fig.  2 ). The Wildhorse Cu–Ag prospect differs in occurring in younger strata above the Kitchener Formation of the Purcell Supergroup (Eagle Plains Resources  40 ). As mentioned above, Re–Os geochronology of molybdenite intergrown with Cu sulfides from a prospect in the Creston Formation, ~ 50 km southeast of the Sullivan deposit, has yielded a date of 1043 ± 6 Ma, reflecting fluid flow and mineralization during the waning stages of the 1150 to 980 Ma Grenvillian orogeny (Perelló et al.  105 ).

sections.heading: Gold-quartz veins
paragraphs: Gold-bearing quartz veins within Belt-Purcell strata are known both in southeastern British Columbia and northern Idaho. On the Canadian side of the border the Gold Shear property, ~ 40 km south of the Sullivan mine, contains several shear-hosted, high-grade quartz veins in the middle Aldridge Formation including the David gold zone with values of up to 25.1 g/t Au over 2.1 m in one drill hole (PJX Resources, Inc.  106 ). These gold-quartz veins are difficult to classify without more detailed studies but likely have either an orogenic or intrusion-related origin, the latter model supported by the occurrence of Cretaceous intrusions within several kilometers of the prospects (Soloviev  135 ).

In northern Idaho, gold deposits of the Murray district (Fig.  1 ) comprise gold-quartz veins with minor Ag, Zn, Pb, Cu and W (McLachlin  96 ; Brown  27 ). The largest, the Golden Chest deposit, has measured + indicated resources of 1.23 Mt at an average grade of 3.52 g/t Au (Idaho Strategic Resources, Inc.  75 ). Most veins at the Golden Chest deposit are banded, but others are brecciated or massive; gold is closely associated with pyrite, galena, sphalerite, and chalcopyrite, and locally with arsenopyrite or scheelite, in a quartz-dominant gangue with minor chlorite, carbonate, muscovite, and feldspar (Brown  27 ; Idaho Strategic Resources, Inc.  75 ). Veins occur in the Prichard Formation, about 16 km north of the Coeur d’Alene district, suggesting a possible relationship to the Mesoproterozoic Ag–Pb–Zn veins there. This hypothesis is supported by mineralogically similar gold ores in the New Jersey gold mine in the western part of the Coeur d’Alene district (Brown  27 ), and by Pb-isotope values for galena from the Murray district that form an array together with Coeur d’Alene Pb-isotope data for tetrahedrite and siderite from silver-rich veins in the Silver belt and for stibnite from antimony veins (Leach et al.  87 ). In contrast, McLachlin ( 96 ) proposed a reduced, intrusion-related gold model for the Murray district veins, based on their proximity (4–6 km) to Cretaceous monzonite intrusions, elevated As, W, and Te concentrations, and occurrence in fluid inclusions of low-salinity CO 2 –H 2 O fluids. However, these metals and fluid compositions are also common in orogenic gold deposits (e.g., Goldfarb and Pitcairn  56 ), raising the possibility of a genetic link between the gold-quartz veins of the Murray district and the East Kootenay or Grenvillian orogenies. Geochronological studies using arsenopyrite (Re–Os), carbonate or scheelite (Sm–Nd, U–Pb), or muscovite ( 40 Ar/ 39 Ar) could prove fruitful in discriminating among these diverse genetic models.

In the York district of western Montana, large stratabound, gold-bearing quartz reefs in the Greyson Formation of the Missoula Group have potential large resources but are likely Cretaceous in age based on a K–Ar age of 89.0 ± 3.2 Ma obtained on hydrothermal K-feldspar (Christiansen et al.  30 ). As a result, these deposits are not discussed further.

sections.heading: Pb–Zn–Ag–(Cu–Au) veins
paragraphs: The large St. Eugene Pb–Zn–Ag vein in southeastern British Columbia (Fig.  1 ) has a past production of 1.48 Mt at an average grade of 7.66% Pb, 0.98% Zn, 124 g/t Ag, and 0.05 g/t Au (Lydon  91 ). This 3.3 km-long vein differs from the majority of other polymetallic veins in the region in being metamorphosed, with textures and Pb-isotope values that indicate formation prior to the 1379 to 1325 Ma East Kootenay orogeny (Beaudoin  12 ; Joncas and Beaudoin  81 ; Paiement et al.  103 ). The smaller Vine deposit in this region (Fig.  1 ) is a pre-metamorphic massive sulfide vein in strata of the middle Aldridge Formation with proven + probable reserves (non-NI 43–101 compliant) of 1.3 Mt at an average grade of 3.12% Pb, 3.12% Zn, 0.11% Cu, 36.3 g/t Ag, and 2.2 g/t Au (Höy and Pighin  70 ; PJX Resources Inc. 2025).

Other polymetallic veins in the region differ in mineralogy and Pb-isotopes and are interpreted to be much younger. Among these veins, two groups are recognized on the basis of dominant metals, Pb–Ag–Cu–Au and Ag–Pb–Zn, both of which likely formed during Cretaceous to Paleocene metamorphism and tectonism (Paiement et al.  103 ) and hence are not discussed further. The Estella mine (Fig.  1 ) produced 109,518 t of Pb–Zn–Cu–Ag–Au ore from 1951 to 1967 from a vein system in strata of the Middle Aldridge Formation (Höy  69 ; British Columbia Ministry of Energy, Mines and Petroleum Resources  25 ),

sections.heading: Au–Cu–(Ag) in veins and breccias
paragraphs: The Bull River vein deposit, 60 km southeast of the Sullivan mine, contains a NI-43-101 indicated resource of 2.26 Mt at an average grade of 1.80% Cu, 15.3 g/t Ag, and 0.42 g/t Au (Canadian Critical Minerals, Inc.  29 ). This 1200-m-long vein, within a thrust fault that cuts strata of the middle Aldridge Formation, contains Fe-sulfides and chalcopyrite with minor galena, sphalerite, arsenopyrite, cobaltite, and gold in a siderite ± quartz gangue (Höy et al.  73 ; Canadian Critical Minerals, Inc.  29 ). The age of this vein is unknown.

Au–Cu deposits and prospects of the Iron Range in southeastern British Columbia (Fig.  1 ) consist of iron oxides (hematite + minor magnetite), pyrite and chalcopyrite, together with locally high gold (up to 51.5 g/t over 7 m) in veins and breccias within part of a 90-km-long fault zone (Stinson and Brown  142 ; Eagle Plains Resources  40 ). This fault zone and the contained mineralization are hosted entirely in the Purcell Supergroup. Based on geologic and geochemical features, including albite-quartz alteration zones and Ti + V vs. Ni/(Cr + Mn) contents of magnetite, the Iron Range deposits could be part of a Mesoproterozoic IOCG mineralizing system (Galicki et al.  45 ). However, the presence of a large Cretaceous plutons ~ 10 km from these Au±(Cu) deposits and prospects, and Cretaceous paleomagnetic pole positions for magnetite (Galicki et al.  45 ), suggests that other models for mineralization are plausible including by metamorphic or magmatic-hydrothermal fluids.

sections.heading: Pegmatite-hosted rare metals (Be, Sn, Nb, Ta, REE)
paragraphs: Some Proterozoic pegmatites in southeastern British Columbia have concentrations of Be, Sn, Nb, Ta, or REE (Fig.  1 ). The 1.36 Ga Hellroaring Creek stock has associated pegmatites with a U–Pb zircon age of 1335 ± 5 Ma (McFarlane  95 ) that contain beryl, cassiterite, and columbite (Brown  28 ; Soloviev  136 ). Undated pegmatites related to the Greenland Creek granitic pluton, ~ 40 km to the north (Fig.  1 ), have multiple occurrences of beryl (Brown  28 ).

On the northern margin of the Idaho cobalt belt, a pegmatite within the Big Deer Creek megacrystic granite contains LREE in abundant allanite (Shockey  125 ). This pegmatite is assumed to have an age similar to that of the host granite, which has been dated via U–Pb zircon at 1377 ± 4 Ma (Aleinikoff et al.  2 ). This rare-metal pegmatite, like those in southeastern British Columbia, were emplaced during the 1379 to 1325 Ma East Kootenay orogeny.

sections.heading: Carbonatite-related REE–Nb–(Mo)
paragraphs: In westernmost Montana, numerous small bodies of carbonatite containing REE, Nb, and minor Mo mineralization have been known for over six decades (Crowley  35 ; Heinrich and Levinson  65 ). These bodies form dikes and veins within metasedimentary and metaigneous rocks and are generally foliated, hence mineralization predates at least one tectonic event. Major minerals are barite, apatite, columbite, euxenite, fersmite, ancylite, monazite, allanite, and bastnäsite in a quartz-carbonate-barite gangue (Gammons  46 ). Recent exploration work has focused on the Sheep Creek and Woods Creek deposits (U.S. Critical Materials Corporation  151 ; Integral Metals Corporation  76 ). The Sheep Creek deposit (Fig.  1 ), which cuts 1.37 Ga metaigneous rocks, has Re–Os dates on molybdenite of 147.9 ± 0.6, 109.8 ± 0.4 and 108.0 ± 0.4 Ma, and Th–Pb dates on monazite of ~ 149 to 145 Ma; the former robust results for molybdenite establish a Mesozoic rather than a Proterozoic age of carbonatite formation (Gammons et al.  48 ). However, one or more older Proterozoic ages for these carbonatites cannot be ruled out, because of multistage mineralization in the region and the Grenvillian ages of 1055 ± 4 Ma on molybdenite and up to 1000 Ma on monazite obtained for the Th–REE–(Cu) veins nearby in the Lemhi Pass district (Gillerman et al.  52 ).

Carbonatites also occur in northern Idaho in the Mineral Hill district north of the Idaho cobalt belt and south of the Sheep Creek deposit (Fig.  1 ; Kaiser  82 ; Anderson  3 ; Gillerman  50 ). Several mineralized bodies are documented that contain abundant monazite, bastnäsite, and xenotime in a carbonate-rich gangue. In the high-grade Lower Roberts prospect, ~ 500 m long and up to 3 m wide, analysis of eight whole-rock samples shows 20.8 to 34.1 wt % ΣREE oxides (Idaho Strategic Resources, Inc.  74 ). These carbonate bodies, and contained minerals, are as yet undated.

sections.heading: Secular evolution of mineralization in the Belt-Purcell Basin
paragraphs: A secular plot of geological and metallogenic events in the Belt-Purcell Basin shows a large age range from ~ 1500 to ~ 50 Ma (Fig.  12 ). Mineralization within this basin produced a diversity of deposit types and commodities including base metals, precious metals, ferrous metals, rare earth metals, and high-field strength metals. Based on geochronological and geological evidence, major mineralization occurred during (1) sedimentation and early diagenesis (Sullivan Pb–Zn–Ag and Black Butte Cu–Co–Ag deposits); (2) late diagenesis (Spar Lake Cu–Ag deposit), Coeur d’Alene Pb–Zn–Ag–(Cu) deposits; (3) the East Kootenay orogeny at 1379 to 1325 Ma (Idaho cobalt belt Co–Cu–Au–(Bi–Y–REE), Coeur d’Alene and St. Eugene Pb–Zn–Ag–(Cu) deposits, Murray district Au-quartz, pegmatite Be–Sn–Nb–Ta–REE (Hellroaring Creek and Big Deer Creek stocks); (4) the Grenvillian orogeny at 1150 to 980 Ma (Creston Formation Cu–Ag, Coeur d’Alene Pb–Zn–Ag–(Cu), Lemhi Pass Th–REE–(Cu); and (5) orogeny during the Cretaceous Period (Coeur d’Alene Pb–Zn–Ag–(Cu) district, York Au-quartz, carbonatite REE–Nb–(Mo) at the Sheep Creek deposit). This compilation, supported by high-precision geochronology, documents an especially significant role for the East Kootenay orogeny, geologically and economically. If most of the stratabound deposits of the Idaho cobalt belt and polymetallic vein ores formed during this orogeny, then related magmatic and tectonothermal events (McMechan and Price  98 ; Doughty and Chamberlain  38 ; McFarlane  95 ) have a greater metallogenic significance than previously recognized. Moreover, if the many gold-quartz veins in the region are of Mesoproterozoic age, then additional importance is linked to the East Kootenay orogeny.

Deep-seated basement structures are also important in having controlled some types of mineralization in the Belt-Purcell Basin (Fig.  1 ). Some of these structures, of Paleoproterozoic and possible Archean age, can in many cases be discerned via regional aeromagnetic anomalies (McMechan  97 ). Examples in Canada include the northeast-trending Vulcan structure in which synsedimentary and younger faults governed the locations of the Sullivan Pb–Zn–Ag deposit, as well as Ag–Pb–Zn and Au veins to the south (Price and Sears  108 ; Box et al.  21 ; PJX Resources, Inc.  106 ). In northern Idaho, the northwest-trending Lewis and Clark tectonic zone, and contained internal faults, localized vein mineralization in the Coeur d’Alene district (White  156 ). Farther south, the Great Falls tectonic zone contains polymetallic deposits of the Idaho cobalt belt and the carbonatite at the Sheep Creek deposit (Box et al.  21 ). Tectonic reactivations of these and other basement structures were likely fundamentally important in promoting repeated mineralization within the same deposit, such as the Coeur d’Alene district veins for which radiometric dating provides strong evidence of episodic mineralization for ~ 1500 m.y. (Fig.  12 ).

An important unanswered question is why the Belt-Purcell Basin is endowed with large metal deposits and districts such as Sullivan (Pb–Zn–Ag), Coeur d’Alene (Ag–Pb–Zn–Cu), and Spar Lake-Rock Creek-Montanore (Cu–Ag). Although radiogenic isotope data (Pb, Sr, Nd) point to multiple source reservoirs, a major source of metals appears to be the metasedimentary rocks of the basin (Beaudoin  13 ; Rosenberg and Larson  115 ; Slack et al.  130 ; Panneerselvam et al.  104 ). Since the western half of the basin derived its detrital load from a since-rifted continental source in Australia-Antarctica (e.g., Armistead et al.  10 ), the major mineral deposits in the western half of the Belt-Purcell Basin (Sullivan, Coeur d’Alene, Spar Lake-Rock Creek-Montanore) thus might have their metal load derived from non-Laurentian detritus.

Additional studies could help to improve our understanding of the complex multistage processes that formed the diversity of deposit types present in the Belt-Purcell Basin. Suggested avenues of research include (1) better understanding of the geometry and evolution of basement structures in the region; (2) more high-precision geochronology to rigorously date mineralization, tectonic events, and metamorphism; and (3) additional geochemical studies (fluid inclusions, stable and radiogenic isotopes) covering the range of deposit types. Such work could aid mineral exploration and resource assessment throughout the Belt-Purcell Basin.
